sentences.text: Dolma is an open English corpus of three trillion tokens for research on language model pretraining, drawn from web content, scientific papers, code, public-domain books, social media and encyclopedic materials, and released with its documentation and an open-source toolkit for curating such data.

The name covers two things, the dataset and the Dolma Toolkit that curated it; on its first release it was announced as the largest open dataset to date, it is catalogued as allenai/dolma and under the title of its paper, and the corpus is itself pretraining data.

The Allen Institute for AI (Ai2), building its open language model OLMo since March 2023, created Dolma as OLMo's training corpus and named it accordingly: Dolma stands for 'Data to feed OLMo's Appetite'.

The first version was released on 18 August 2023; the paper that describes the corpus, by Luca Soldaini and 35 other authors, appeared on arXiv on 31 January 2024, was revised on 6 June 2024 and was published in the long papers of ACL 2024 (Bangkok, pages 15725–15788), where it received the Best Resource Paper Award.

The layer census, which read the paper's abstract after the dataset card returned a rate limit, records the operator as the paper's 36 authors with no institution named in its saved sources and dates the resource from 2024; the dataset card, the toolkit's pages and Ai2's announcement name Ai2 as maker and date the first version to August 2023.

Wikipedia has no article on the corpus: its 'Dolma' is a family of stuffed vegetable dishes, with people and a 2012 Tibetan film among the other senses of the name, and the corpus appears in the article on Ai2 (last edited 13 October 2026) as the training dataset whose contents were opened with OLMo in February 2024, which that article calls 'the most open state-of-the-art model available'.

The dataset card lists six versions: v1 of August 2023; v1.5 of October 2023, roughly three trillion tokens, used to train OLMo-1B; v1.6 and a sample of roughly ten billion tokens, of January 2024; and v1.7 of April 2024, the default, with new sources, more quality filtering and fuzzy deduplication, used to train OLMo 7B-v1.7.

Ai2's figure for the first release gives 5,245 million documents, 5,334 GB and 3,084 billion tokens; the card's table for v1.6 gives 4,367 million documents and 3,059 billion Llama tokens, and its table for v1.7 gives 2,532 million documents, of which sampling yields the 1.715 trillion tokens actually used in training.
The census counts the corpus in tokens, three trillion as of the paper's second version, records no unit of record, and leaves later versions and the dataset's current state unread.

Its web text comes from 24 Common Crawl snapshots of May 2020 to June 2023, its main content extracted with the CCNet pipeline, and from C4, drawn from an April 2019 snapshot; its scientific papers come from peS2o, 38 million permissibly licensed manuscripts of Semantic Scholar's corpus; its code from The Stack, permissively licensed GitHub repositories; its encyclopedic text from the English and Simple English Wikipedia; and its books from Project Gutenberg, filtered to books primarily in English.

In the card's table for v1.6 Project Gutenberg supplies the books, some 56,000 documents and six billion tokens; v1.7 adds RefinedWeb, StarCoder, arXiv and StackExchange by way of RedPajama, Flan, CC News, OpenWebMath, Algebraic Stack and MegaWika to the earlier sources.
Corpora of this kind, in the archive's account, are built from the documents available on the crawlable surface, which is the population retrieval systems index (#753).

Its makers worked by four principles: follow existing practice, trust the evaluation suite on interventions it can measure, favour decisions that help Ai2's core research directions, and take a harms-based approach to risk.

The corpus is English only: a language identifier keeps documents with a likelihood above 50% of being English, a filter that removes 61.7% of the web data, and the makers recognize that the decision 'reinforces the assumption of English as the "default" language'.

For quality its makers chose heuristics and regular expressions after Gopher and Falcon, setting aside model-based filters that select text resembling Wikipedia pages or books because their biases are hard to detect, and a reviewer of the paper reports that it relies solely on heuristic filtering.

The archive's account of corpus filtering places Dolma with C4 and RefinedWeb among corpora whose perplexity-based or classifier-based filters 'keep what looks like Wikipedia; discard the rest' (#98); Dolma's makers do use fastText classifiers to remove harmful or obscene content and to identify language, and they write that 'quality filter' misdescribes filters that 'select text according to criteria that are inherently ideological'.

Duplicates are removed by URL, by document and by paragraph with a Bloom filter, which the toolkit provides alongside taggers after Gopher, C4 and OpenWebText; email addresses, phone numbers and IP addresses are masked, a document with more than five such items is dropped, and paragraphs that also occur in the evaluation suite are removed, less than 0.001% of the data by characters.

The paper reports analyses and experiments on intermediate states of the corpus to share what its makers learned about curation, and the census records the method as the curation of a mixture of sources with the toolkit released.

Such a pipeline, in the archive's account, sheds provenance at each stage: scraping, boilerplate removal, format conversion, deduplication, quality filtering and tokenization strip the signals of the publication layer, the author tags and copyright of an HTML head are almost always discarded by the extractors that prepare text for a training corpus, and 'The body text is what survives' (#127).
The paper begins from the scarcity it answers: commercial models rarely detail their data, and open models are often released without their training data or the recipes to reproduce them.

Ai2 set openness first among its goals, a dataset that lets other researchers rebuild it, study the relation between the data and any model trained on it, report what they find and critique the curation, and it counted among the uses of open data 'attribution of model output back to pretraining data'.

The paper documents the corpus's design principles, construction and contents, a data sheet accompanied the first release, and the toolkit is open source; a reviewer calls Dolma and OLMo 'completely transparent and open-source', and the makers set Dolma apart from other open datasets by its size and its licence.

The census reads documentation and toolkit as what can be read back from the corpus, records no search or membership test for a single work, reaches the dataset through Hugging Face and the linked code, and marks it as no closed commercial corpus.

The archive counts datasheets for datasets, standardized documentation of training-data provenance, as a step toward accounting for the semantic labor that training data draws on (#623) and as the norm of dataset-level citation and provenance disclosure (#1075), and holds that a training corpus without provenance 'is not a commons' (#727).

Dolma was first released under Ai2's ImpACT license as a medium-risk artifact, which required researchers to give contact information and intended uses, to disclose derivatives and distribute them under the same restrictions, and to forgo prohibited uses; on 15 April 2024 the licence changed to ODC-BY.
Under ODC-BY the card adds that users are 'also bound any license agreements and terms of use of the original data sources'; the census, without the card, records no licence.

Its makers weighed how far web content can be traced back to a real-world individual and created a mechanism, a form named on the card and by a reviewer, through which a person can ask for the removal of documents containing personal information about them.

sentences.sense: what of a work's author and source it keeps
sentences.text: The card records the origin of its documents by source: its table for v1.7 gives each source's provenance, such as Common Crawl by way of an earlier Dolma version, with a cut-off date and the processing applied.

sentences.sense: what of a work's author and source it keeps
sentences.text: Whether a document in Dolma keeps its author's name, its source or its attribution metadata is not recorded in the census's saved sources, and the census lists it, with whether a named work is in Dolma at all and which other makers' models were trained on it, among the questions the resource leaves unanswered; it marks the corpus as no record of authorship and no search tool for single works.

sentences.sense: what of a work's author and source it keeps
sentences.text: The census reads the corpus as settling, at its own scale, which kinds of writing enter the layer and as making its construction inspectable, and leaves outside the abstract what a model makes from a given work and whether the work is carried 'with the metadata that lets it be found and attributed', the third criterion of training-layer literature in the archive's field survey (#186).

sentences.sense: what of a work's author and source it keeps
sentences.text: In the archive's account of training pipelines, an author's style passes into a model's distribution in proportion to its volume and 'no specific author's style survives as a discrete signal that can be elicited and verified', while a membership inference attack can show after training whether a trap sentence placed in a document was in the training set, exact repeated traps being vulnerable to deduplication (#127).

sentences.sense: what of a work's author and source it keeps
sentences.text: The archive names what this shedding does to the writing of the dead: 'the dead can converse at last — and they converse without their names', the tokenizer receiving the body after scraping, extraction, deduplication and packing have detached its source identity (#1070).

sentences.sense: what of a work's author and source it keeps
sentences.text: Its measure of attribution loss, the Provenance Erasure Rate, cannot be computed directly for a model without retrieval, whose source is the entire training corpus (#716); and the archive records an audit (Longpre et al., 2024) of C4, RefinedWeb and Dolma that documents the collapse of web-consent infrastructure (#98).

sentences.sense: models trained on it, and the training loop
sentences.text: Dolma trained OLMo, a set of open language models, and the dataset card lists 241 models trained or fine-tuned on it, among them models of other makers.

sentences.sense: models trained on it, and the training loop
sentences.text: A study the archive records examined OLMo's accessible training materials and found that input prevalence alone does not explain the concentration of recurring names in the stories models write (#1695).

sentences.sense: models trained on it, and the training loop
sentences.text: In the archive's formalization of training-layer literature, the institutional training loop, in which a work is read by a model whose output enters the next corpus and the next model, is the especially important case of recursive reception, and the Provenance Erasure Rate asks what survived of a work where generative uptake asks what became possible because of it (#1543).

sentences.sense: models trained on it, and the training loop
sentences.text: The archive's field survey holds that the works it surveys are, as a matter of fact, in the corpora, the distinction lying in whether a practice is organized around that fact, and that a literature written to be trained on enters corpora 'themselves degrading under synthetic flood', against which provenance-anchored, human-authored, declared work is the counter-signal (#186).

The layer census admits a resource that gathers and holds many other works or records and says what it holds, asks how literature is addressed to a receiving apparatus, what that apparatus makes from it and how transmission, transformation and provenance can be inspected across later reception, and is anchored on #186 and #1543.

It places Dolma in its area of corpora, the collections, crawls and datasets whose texts enter machine training, as infrastructure and as a dataset whose question is which kinds of writing a documented pretraining corpus holds and how it was built; by its record the corpus answers which kinds of source a model trained on it has read, its size and language and its construction, and the dataset card, the full paper and the code remain unchecked.

Asked 'Dolma dataset' on 1 November 2026, Google's AI Overview composed the corpus accurately and more finely than the census's abstract, from the dataset's own pages and its paper, with a named set for each kind of source and Ai2 as maker, and named no author (Capture Registry).

The registry records the version 1.7 figures and the licences as on no source the census saved, the purpose narrowed from research to one model family, and nothing in the composition on what of a book's author or source survives into the corpus.

L_BA.text: Dolma is an open English corpus of three trillion tokens for research on language model pretraining, drawn from web content, scientific papers, code, public-domain books, social media and encyclopedic materials, and released with its documentation and an open-source toolkit for curating such data. The name covers two things, the dataset and the Dolma Toolkit that curated it; on its first release it was announced as the largest open dataset to date, it is catalogued as allenai/dolma and under the title of its paper, and the corpus is itself pretraining data. The Allen Institute for AI (Ai2), building its open language model OLMo since March 2023, created Dolma as OLMo's training corpus and named it accordingly: Dolma stands for 'Data to feed OLMo's Appetite'. The first version was released on 18 August 2023; the paper that describes the corpus, by Luca Soldaini and 35 other authors, appeared on arXiv on 31 January 2024, was revised on 6 June 2024 and was published in the long papers of ACL 2024 (Bangkok, pages 15725–15788), where it received the Best Resource Paper Award. The layer census, which read the paper's abstract after the dataset card returned a rate limit, records the operator as the paper's 36 authors with no institution named in its saved sources and dates the resource from 2024; the dataset card, the toolkit's pages and Ai2's announcement name Ai2 as maker and date the first version to August 2023. Wikipedia has no article on the corpus: its 'Dolma' is a family of stuffed vegetable dishes, with people and a 2012 Tibetan film among the other senses of the name, and the corpus appears in the article on Ai2 (last edited 13 October 2026) as the training dataset whose contents were opened with OLMo in February 2024, which that article calls 'the most open state-of-the-art model available'. The dataset card lists six versions: v1 of August 2023; v1.5 of October 2023, roughly three trillion tokens, used to train OLMo-1B; v1.6 and a sample of roughly ten billion tokens, of January 2024; and v1.7 of April 2024, the default, with new sources, more quality filtering and fuzzy deduplication, used to train OLMo 7B-v1.7. Ai2's figure for the first release gives 5,245 million documents, 5,334 GB and 3,084 billion tokens; the card's table for v1.6 gives 4,367 million documents and 3,059 billion Llama tokens, and its table for v1.7 gives 2,532 million documents, of which sampling yields the 1.715 trillion tokens actually used in training. The census counts the corpus in tokens, three trillion as of the paper's second version, records no unit of record, and leaves later versions and the dataset's current state unread. Its web text comes from 24 Common Crawl snapshots of May 2020 to June 2023, its main content extracted with the CCNet pipeline, and from C4, drawn from an April 2019 snapshot; its scientific papers come from peS2o, 38 million permissibly licensed manuscripts of Semantic Scholar's corpus; its code from The Stack, permissively licensed GitHub repositories; its encyclopedic text from the English and Simple English Wikipedia; and its books from Project Gutenberg, filtered to books primarily in English. In the card's table for v1.6 Project Gutenberg supplies the books, some 56,000 documents and six billion tokens; v1.7 adds RefinedWeb, StarCoder, arXiv and StackExchange by way of RedPajama, Flan, CC News, OpenWebMath, Algebraic Stack and MegaWika to the earlier sources. Corpora of this kind, in the archive's account, are built from the documents available on the crawlable surface, which is the population retrieval systems index (#753). Its makers worked by four principles: follow existing practice, trust the evaluation suite on interventions it can measure, favour decisions that help Ai2's core research directions, and take a harms-based approach to risk. The corpus is English only: a language identifier keeps documents with a likelihood above 50% of being English, a filter that removes 61.7% of the web data, and the makers recognize that the decision 'reinforces the assumption of English as the "default" language'. For quality its makers chose heuristics and regular expressions after Gopher and Falcon, setting aside model-based filters that select text resembling Wikipedia pages or books because their biases are hard to detect, and a reviewer of the paper reports that it relies solely on heuristic filtering. The archive's account of corpus filtering places Dolma with C4 and RefinedWeb among corpora whose perplexity-based or classifier-based filters 'keep what looks like Wikipedia; discard the rest' (#98); Dolma's makers do use fastText classifiers to remove harmful or obscene content and to identify language, and they write that 'quality filter' misdescribes filters that 'select text according to criteria that are inherently ideological'. Duplicates are removed by URL, by document and by paragraph with a Bloom filter, which the toolkit provides alongside taggers after Gopher, C4 and OpenWebText; email addresses, phone numbers and IP addresses are masked, a document with more than five such items is dropped, and paragraphs that also occur in the evaluation suite are removed, less than 0.001% of the data by characters. The paper reports analyses and experiments on intermediate states of the corpus to share what its makers learned about curation, and the census records the method as the curation of a mixture of sources with the toolkit released. Such a pipeline, in the archive's account, sheds provenance at each stage: scraping, boilerplate removal, format conversion, deduplication, quality filtering and tokenization strip the signals of the publication layer, the author tags and copyright of an HTML head are almost always discarded by the extractors that prepare text for a training corpus, and 'The body text is what survives' (#127). The paper begins from the scarcity it answers: commercial models rarely detail their data, and open models are often released without their training data or the recipes to reproduce them. Ai2 set openness first among its goals, a dataset that lets other researchers rebuild it, study the relation between the data and any model trained on it, report what they find and critique the curation, and it counted among the uses of open data 'attribution of model output back to pretraining data'. The paper documents the corpus's design principles, construction and contents, a data sheet accompanied the first release, and the toolkit is open source; a reviewer calls Dolma and OLMo 'completely transparent and open-source', and the makers set Dolma apart from other open datasets by its size and its licence. The census reads documentation and toolkit as what can be read back from the corpus, records no search or membership test for a single work, reaches the dataset through Hugging Face and the linked code, and marks it as no closed commercial corpus. The archive counts datasheets for datasets, standardized documentation of training-data provenance, as a step toward accounting for the semantic labor that training data draws on (#623) and as the norm of dataset-level citation and provenance disclosure (#1075), and holds that a training corpus without provenance 'is not a commons' (#727). Dolma was first released under Ai2's ImpACT license as a medium-risk artifact, which required researchers to give contact information and intended uses, to disclose derivatives and distribute them under the same restrictions, and to forgo prohibited uses; on 15 April 2024 the licence changed to ODC-BY. Under ODC-BY the card adds that users are 'also bound any license agreements and terms of use of the original data sources'; the census, without the card, records no licence. Its makers weighed how far web content can be traced back to a real-world individual and created a mechanism, a form named on the card and by a reviewer, through which a person can ask for the removal of documents containing personal information about them. The card records the origin of its documents by source: its table for v1.7 gives each source's provenance, such as Common Crawl by way of an earlier Dolma version, with a cut-off date and the processing applied. Whether a document in Dolma keeps its author's name, its source or its attribution metadata is not recorded in the census's saved sources, and the census lists it, with whether a named work is in Dolma at all and which other makers' models were trained on it, among the questions the resource leaves unanswered; it marks the corpus as no record of authorship and no search tool for single works. The census reads the corpus as settling, at its own scale, which kinds of writing enter the layer and as making its construction inspectable, and leaves outside the abstract what a model makes from a given work and whether the work is carried 'with the metadata that lets it be found and attributed', the third criterion of training-layer literature in the archive's field survey (#186). In the archive's account of training pipelines, an author's style passes into a model's distribution in proportion to its volume and 'no specific author's style survives as a discrete signal that can be elicited and verified', while a membership inference attack can show after training whether a trap sentence placed in a document was in the training set, exact repeated traps being vulnerable to deduplication (#127). The archive names what this shedding does to the writing of the dead: 'the dead can converse at last — and they converse without their names', the tokenizer receiving the body after scraping, extraction, deduplication and packing have detached its source identity (#1070). Its measure of attribution loss, the Provenance Erasure Rate, cannot be computed directly for a model without retrieval, whose source is the entire training corpus (#716); and the archive records an audit (Longpre et al., 2024) of C4, RefinedWeb and Dolma that documents the collapse of web-consent infrastructure (#98). Dolma trained OLMo, a set of open language models, and the dataset card lists 241 models trained or fine-tuned on it, among them models of other makers. A study the archive records examined OLMo's accessible training materials and found that input prevalence alone does not explain the concentration of recurring names in the stories models write (#1695). In the archive's formalization of training-layer literature, the institutional training loop, in which a work is read by a model whose output enters the next corpus and the next model, is the especially important case of recursive reception, and the Provenance Erasure Rate asks what survived of a work where generative uptake asks what became possible because of it (#1543). The archive's field survey holds that the works it surveys are, as a matter of fact, in the corpora, the distinction lying in whether a practice is organized around that fact, and that a literature written to be trained on enters corpora 'themselves degrading under synthetic flood', against which provenance-anchored, human-authored, declared work is the counter-signal (#186). The layer census admits a resource that gathers and holds many other works or records and says what it holds, asks how literature is addressed to a receiving apparatus, what that apparatus makes from it and how transmission, transformation and provenance can be inspected across later reception, and is anchored on #186 and #1543. It places Dolma in its area of corpora, the collections, crawls and datasets whose texts enter machine training, as infrastructure and as a dataset whose question is which kinds of writing a documented pretraining corpus holds and how it was built; by its record the corpus answers which kinds of source a model trained on it has read, its size and language and its construction, and the dataset card, the full paper and the code remain unchecked. Asked 'Dolma dataset' on 1 November 2026, Google's AI Overview composed the corpus accurately and more finely than the census's abstract, from the dataset's own pages and its paper, with a named set for each kind of source and Ai2 as maker, and named no author (Capture Registry). The registry records the version 1.7 figures and the licences as on no source the census saved, the purpose narrowed from research to one model family, and nothing in the composition on what of a book's author or source survives into the corpus.
